title: Bending reality with Gaussian splats and VR
cardTitle: Bending reality with Gaussian splats and VR
summary: A VR experiment in making people question what they see. We used a scanned hallway and Codex to turn familiar surroundings into an impossible space.
coverAlt: Calibrated VR experience with a scanned hallway and shifting geometry

metadata.label: My role
metadata.value: Experience direction, spatial interaction and AI-assisted prototyping

metadata.label: Tools
metadata.value: Codex, Gaussian splats, WebXR, Three.js, Meta Quest 3, SteamVR / Steam Link

blocks.title: A familiar space made unreliable
blocks.body: We wanted to bend reality until participants could no longer trust their eyes. Could we do it without modelling the environment or writing the code ourselves? Gaussian splats gave us the captured space; Codex helped turn our directions into interactions.

blocks.title: From a normal hallway to an impossible space where you can't trust your eyes
blocks.body: We began with a question about perception, captured a real hallway, then built the experience one interaction at a time. Calibration came first: the illusion needed a believable starting point.

blocks.title: Early experiment: virtual characters anchored to real people
blocks.body: We explored mapping virtual characters onto real people, so reaching out in VR would mean touching someone physically present. We later shifted focus to transforming the hallway itself.

blocks.title: Aligning the digital copy with the real hallway
blocks.body: Two controller landmarks aligned the scan with the physical space. We checked its scale against a door frame and moved to SteamVR and Steam Link when the original streaming route failed.

blocks.title: Shaping Gaussian splats through agentic coding
blocks.body: I started with a cube and a hallway rotation, then directed Codex through prompts and annotated screenshots. It understood where I wanted to cut, move and connect the splats. I found this more effective than manipulating them by hand with the tools available to me.

blocks.title: Choosing a believable visual language
blocks.body: We left out a creature that looked too synthetic. Real scanned objects made the impossible transformations more convincing; the final collapse broke the hallway into uneven patches before dissolving into white.

blocks.title: A two-minute experience that drew a crowd
blocks.body: People queued to try calibrated, with each experience lasting about two minutes. We recorded most participants both in the physical hallway and from their view inside VR, capturing how they moved and reacted as the world around them changed.

blocks.title: From concept to 15 participants in one week
blocks.body: We built calibrated in just one week and tested it with 15 people. All participant sessions ran without technical difficulties.

blocks.title: Convincing realism and enthusiastic reactions
blocks.body: Participants were amazed by how real the experience felt. Some mistook the position of the door and bumped into a wall, showing how strongly the virtual space had shifted their sense of the physical hallway. The feedback was overwhelmingly positive, with people comparing the experience to Inception and describing it as both amazing and disorienting.

blocks.title: Finding direction through pivots
blocks.body: I really enjoyed the shifts in direction. We began with the idea of mapping characters onto people and ended up making the hallway itself feel impossible. The idea changed, but the intention stayed consistent: to unsettle the relationship between what someone sees and what they physically feel. Each pivot was a chance to reconsider how we could create that feeling.

blocks.title: Aligning intentions, agents and people
blocks.body: It felt like half the work was alignment: agreeing on what we wanted people to experience, communicating that intention to the coding agents, and keeping a shared understanding within the team. Building and testing helped us make those intentions concrete. Directing the work meant continually interpreting the results together and deciding what to change next.

blocks.title: More room for parallel experimentation
blocks.body: Four people shared one computer and headset, which sometimes held up the work. For a next iteration, we would use two setups so building and testing could happen in parallel.
